title: Paste a generated repair payload — never re-type it; the hand is the untrusted transport
statement: When a repair payload has been generated from canonical source data, PASTE it into the tool call — never re-type or re-transcribe it. The hand is the untrusted transport: re-typing reintroduces exactly the class of error the generator existed to remove. And end every repair spanning more than one row with an INDEPENDENT re-read that re-derives each expected value from its source, because care does not catch a transcription error — only a verifier does.
context: The tamheed 4.2.0 register repair (PE-336; findings_18 §1). Recovering probability and impact for all 23 risk rows, every payload was correctly BUILT BY SCRIPT from data/*.jsonl rather than from entity_query output — the rule that was already on the books, and it was followed. Transcribing the generator's output into the entity_upsert call, I typed RISK-012's probability as `medium` where the stash said H -> high. The generator was right for all 23 rows; the transport corrupted one. What caught it was NOT care — I was being careful, and care missed it — but a verifier that re-read the JSONL after the write and re-derived every expected value from the stash independently, which named the offending row in one line.
recommendation: 1. Build the payload from the canonical files (`data/*.jsonl`), never from an `entity_query` round-trip — the store holds truncated rows and v4 demands full ones. 2. Move it into the call by PASTE, not by hand. 3. Where a paste is structurally impossible — an MCP tool call whose arguments must be composed rather than pasted — treat the composition as untrusted and make step 4 mandatory rather than optional. 4. End any repair over N>1 rows with an independent verifier that re-reads the canonical file and re-derives each expected value from its own source; ASSERT the comparison, never eyeball it. Save a pre-image before the write so the verifier has something to compare against.
rationale: A generator's correctness does not survive manual re-transcription: generation and transport are two steps and only the first is mechanical. The failure is silent by construction — a plausible value in a plausible field — so nothing downstream refuses it, and re-reading your own transcription recruits the same faculty that produced the error. Only a re-derivation from the source has the property that it cannot repeat the mistake, which is why the verifier and not the vigilance is the control.
impact_if_followed: A multi-row repair's correctness rests on two mechanical things — the generator and the verifier — rather than on the hand between them. Demonstrated on the 4.2.0 re-run: scale mismatches NONE, lost stash NONE, titles byte-identical to v1.Risk, milestones 6/6 with the v1 blob preserved. The cost is one extra script. Demonstrated again on 2026-08-15 closing DEF-056: a 3102-character defect title was re-sent and verified verbatim against a pre-image, and the same discipline surfaced a hand-invented `found_in` value that the store's FK then refused.
impact_if_ignored: A silently corrupted row enters an append-only record wearing a plausible value that no gate can refuse. Every mechanical gate here is ROW-LEVEL, which is exactly how the v2.3 migration passed 7/7 while damaging register data at COLUMN level. RISK-012 would have carried a wrong probability into every later risk review, and `risk-liveness` — whose predicate reads probability and impact — would have evaluated the wrong row without failing, the hollow-pass shape all over again.

title: Ask every time — a previously given answer is evidence about the past, never consent for the present
statement: When a decision belongs to the operator, run the interview EVERY time. Do not bank their earlier answers as a starting position, a default, or a shortcut for a later ceremony. An answer given in one context is evidence of what was true then; it is never authorisation for now. Where a record must carry a past answer, mark it explicitly as history that does NOT relieve the next session of asking.
context: 2026-08-16, the first `skill-promote` ceremony. The ceremony was run correctly — candidates clustered, the pinned-lesson graduation warning given, a straw-man offered, and a hard STOP at the operator's cluster pick — and the operator DECLINED. Alongside the decline they answered two of the interview questions (a name, and a level that went against the recommendation). I recorded those in `PE-368` framed as captured 'so the interview is not re-run from scratch'. The operator rejected that framing outright: 'always you must interview me'. Corrected in `PE-369`. Note that nothing was mis-written and no work was authorised wrongly — the damage was entirely in the RECORD, which would have taught the next session to treat a stale answer as a settled starting point.
recommendation: 1. Treat an operator answer as scoped to the moment it was given — the decision it accompanied, and nothing further. 2. Never carry answers forward as inputs to a future interview, even to be 'efficient'; the efficiency comes out of the operator's authority. 3. When a record must preserve what was said, label it HISTORY and state in the same breath that the next session asks again regardless. 4. Read a ceremony prompt's own stop conditions as binding on the RECORD as well as on the actions: honouring a STOP and then writing a shortcut past it into the journal defeats it one session later. 5. When in doubt about whether something is the operator's to decide, ask — the cost of one question is always lower than the cost of an assumed default.
rationale: Banking an answer silently converts a DECISION into a DEFAULT. The next session reads the captured value, treats it as settled, and the interview the ceremony exists to force degrades into a confirmation of something said once about a different moment — the operator is nominally still consulted while their actual choice has been pre-made. This is the same failure the lesson family itself screens for (persisting an answer as if it remained true), arriving through the journal rather than through a lesson row. It is also why interactive ceremonies place their STOPs where they do: the stop is worthless if the record routes around it.
impact_if_followed: Every operator decision is made in the context it actually applies to, and the record stays a description of what happened rather than a set of pre-loaded answers. Ceremonies keep the property they were designed for — that the operator decides at every step — across session boundaries, which is the only place that property can be lost.
impact_if_ignored: A stale preference quietly becomes policy. The most likely concrete harm here: a later session opens the promotion, reads a captured name and level, and writes a `SKILL.md` at a level the operator would no longer choose — having been 'consulted' only to confirm their own months-old answer. Worse, the failure is invisible, because the record will show an interview that appeared to happen.

title: Open the interview the moment a decision or an action is the operator's — never surface a blocker and then stand still. Do the homework first, ask simply with examples, and show the entity with its id.
statement: When something needs the OPERATOR — a decision that is theirs to make, or an action only they can perform — START THE INTERVIEW IMMEDIATELY. Do not report the blocker and wait to be asked. FOUR RULES GOVERN HOW IT IS DONE. (1) DO THE HOMEWORK FIRST: gather the facts, read the code, take the measurement, resolve everything that is resolvable, so the operator is DECIDING rather than researching. Never ask a question whose answer is already in the repository. (2) ASK CLEARLY AND SIMPLY, WITH EXAMPLES: one decision per question, plain language, and a concrete illustration of what each option means in practice. (3) DISPLAY THE ENTITY WITH ITS ID: quote what the row actually says — its text, severity, status — AND keep the identifier alongside it, so the decision can be made from the message itself while the id remains the handle for looking it up, quoting it back, and tracing it. Neither half alone is enough: an id without content makes the reader fetch the record, and content without an id makes the claim uncheckable. This applies to DEF-, DEC-, ADR-, AC-, RISK- and every other family. (4) ASKING EARLY IS NOT A LICENCE TO REUSE (LL-002): every ceremony still gets its own fresh interview.
context: 2026-08-16, given by the operator during the DEF-078 readiness work. Across that session the agent repeatedly did the right analysis and then STOPPED at the edge of the operator's authority — surfacing the UAT credential rotation (blocked on a stopped instance), the gitleaks allowlist narrowing (blocked on docs triage), and the startup-interlock consequence of DEC-056 d2 — and in each case wrote 'this is your call' and waited instead of putting the question. The operator had to prompt for the interview. Nothing was decided wrongly; the cost was pure latency and an unfinished turn, repeatedly. The same session also showed the presentation failure: blockers were cited as bare identifiers ('DEF-081 is filed high'), which forces the reader to open the register to learn what they are being asked about.
recommendation: 1. The moment a blocker is identified as the operator's, ASK — in the same turn, not the next one. 2. Before asking, exhaust what you can determine yourself: run the command, read the config, take the measurement. An interview that offloads research is worse than none. 3. One decision per question; name the options and show what each looks like in practice. 4. Quote the entity's content inline — severity, status, and the sentence that matters — WITH its id: never the id alone, and never the content alone. 5. Where an option carries a risk the operator has not seen, state it inside the option, not after the answer. 6. If several decisions are pending, batch them into one interview rather than trickling them across turns.
rationale: An agent that identifies an operator decision and then waits has converted a two-minute question into an idle turn, and has quietly made a decision of its own — the decision not to ask yet. The operator experiences this as the work stalling for no stated reason. The homework clause is the load-bearing half: asking early is only valuable if the question is fully prepared, because an interview that hands back unresearched options looks like consultation while transferring the work. And an id-only reference has the same defect at the presentation layer — it appears to inform while requiring the reader to do the retrieval, which in practice means the decision gets made on the agent's summary instead of the record. The id must still travel with the content, though: it is the durable handle that makes the summary checkable against the register and citable afterwards, so quoting content without an id trades one presentation failure for another.
category: operator-interaction; interview; blocking; question-quality; entity-presentation; preparation
impact_if_followed: Operator decisions arrive early, fully prepared, and answerable from the message itself. Blocked work either unblocks in the same turn or is explicitly parked BY THE OPERATOR rather than by the agent's silence. The register is read as content rather than as pointers, so a wrong recommendation is visible at the moment of decision.
impact_if_ignored: Work stalls at exactly the points that matter most — the ones needing authority — and the stall is invisible, because the agent's report reads as complete. The most likely concrete harm: a security item like the outstanding UAT credential rotation sits 'surfaced' across several sessions, each one correctly identifying it and none asking the one question that would close it, while the agent's own status reports show it as known and handled.

title: A package-write commit cannot cite itself - reconcile git against the package by CLASSIFYING the unreferenced commits, never by counting them
statement: When cross-checking git against a Tamheed package, a commit whose entire content IS the package write can never contain a reference to its own sha: the MCP write happens FIRST, and the commit carrying the resulting JSONL is created afterwards, so that sha did not exist when the row was written. The raw 'commits with no recorded binding' set is therefore dominated by commits that are correct by construction. NEVER report that raw set as a finding. Classify every unreferenced commit by the PATHS IT TOUCHES - package-only, memory/docs-only, or production code - and flag ONLY the production-code ones. State the discriminator in the report even when the result is empty, so a clean result is legible as a check that RAN rather than a check that was skipped.
context: 2026-08-17 orientation on the ACMP package (PE-415). The orient-resume instruction asks for 'commits that look like package-relevant work but have no recorded binding'. Substring-matching each of the last 25 shas against data/*.jsonl returned 19 unreferenced - 76% of the window. Reporting that list would have been 18 false alarms, and the prompt's own wording invites the error: a `chore(tamheed)` commit IS package-relevant work under any plain reading. One `git show --name-only` per commit resolved it in a single pass - 18 touched only tamheed-package/**, one touched only a memory file, and the single production-code commit in the window (8eba85a, PR #288) was correctly bound under DW-026. The nearly-made mistake was not a wrong conclusion but a wrong REPORT: handing the operator 19 identifiers to research.
recommendation: 1. Match each commit's short AND full sha against all data/*.jsonl mechanically - never judge from commit messages, which say 'DEF-084' whether or not anything was bound. 2. For every unreferenced commit run `git show --name-only` and bucket by path prefix: tamheed-package/** = self-referentially unbindable, expected clean; memory/docs-only = out of scope; anything under src/ or tests/ = a real candidate. 3. Flag bucket 3 ONLY. 4. Report the discriminator alongside the result - 'none, because every unreferenced commit is a package write, which cannot cite itself' is a check; a bare 'no findings' is indistinguishable from not having looked. 5. Never invent a verdict for a bucket-3 commit: name it and let the operator decide.
rationale: The check's raw output has a systematically high false-positive rate that is a property of the RECORDING PROTOCOL itself, not of the repository's health - package writes are always committed after the fact. An agent that reports the raw set trains the operator to ignore the check. An agent that quietly drops it reports 'no unrecorded work' from a check whose output was never interpreted, which is this project's recorded hollow-pass shape arriving at the reporting layer instead of the test layer. The path-prefix classification is the only step that separates the two, and it costs one `git show` per commit.
impact_if_followed: The git-to-package reconciliation stays a LIVE signal: a genuinely unrecorded code commit is visible against a quiet background instead of buried in a list of expected ones, and an empty result carries its own evidence that the instrument had a subject. Demonstrated on 2026-08-17: 25 commits reduced to exactly one production-code commit, checked, and found already bound.
impact_if_ignored: Two opposite failure modes, both bad. Reported raw, the check cries wolf - 19 of 25 commits flagged here - and the operator learns to skip it, so the one genuinely unbound commit eventually arrives inside a list nobody reads. Suppressed, the report asserts 'no unrecorded work' on the strength of an uninterpreted check; this project already records that a clean scan which cannot prove it had a subject is indistinguishable from a clean codebase (the DEF-039 i18n grep that scanned the renamed token, and DEF-056's two NotContain controls that passed vacuously against a column of nulls).

title: Check the register BEFORE offering the operator an option, not after — 'record it as deliberately unexposed' is a silent retirement when an approved requirement already covers the capability
statement: Before asking the operator to dispose of a capability — wire it, drop it, record it as intentional — search the requirement register for a row that already covers it. An option like 'record as deliberately unexposed' silently PRESUMES the capability is unplanned. If an Approved requirement covers it, choosing that option retires approved, traced work by side effect, and the operator cannot see that unless the check was run first. The register sweep is part of the homework LL-003 rule 1 demands, not a follow-up task: an interview option that has not been checked against the plan is not a prepared question, however well the code was read.
context: 2026-08-17, the DEF-084 interview (PE-418, DEC-057). The code homework was thorough — all eight unreachable methods read in source, every caller grepped, three distinct root causes established — and on that basis the operator was asked whether to wire Topic.Convert and Topic.Reclassify or 'record them as deliberately unexposed'. They chose unexposed. Only afterwards, running the FR-coverage check the advisor prompted for, did FR-030 appear: Approved, priority S, sourced to README section E, already traced WBS-5.7 --implements--> and TEST-018 --tests-->, and covering exactly that conversion capability. Applying the answer as given would have abandoned an approved traced requirement by way of a comment in a test-file allowlist. The answer was NOT applied: the fact was surfaced, the question re-put with FR-030 quoted in full, and the operator chose explicit deferral (DW-030). Nothing was mis-written — the cost was one wasted decision and an interview the operator had to make twice.
recommendation: 1. For every capability an interview will ask about, sweep the requirement register (title + statement + rationale) for it BEFORE composing the question — a regex over the canonical requirements.jsonl takes seconds and reads all rows, not the ones you remember. 2. Also check its trace edges: a requirement with implements/tests edges is PLANNED work with a work item and a test row behind it, which is a much stronger claim on the operator's attention than a bare Approved row. 3. Where a requirement exists, the honest options are build / defer with a trigger / retire via scope-change — 'record as unexposed' is not among them, because it changes the plan without a scope-change row. 4. Where no requirement exists, say so explicitly in the option, because that is itself the decision-relevant fact. 5. If the check is run late and contradicts an answer already given, SURFACE IT AND RE-ASK — never apply the answer and note the discrepancy afterwards.
rationale: An interview transfers a decision to the operator, and it can only do that honestly if the options are true. 'Record it as deliberately unexposed' sounds like a no-op — nothing is built, nothing is deleted — which is exactly why it is dangerous: its real effect, when a requirement exists, is to retire that requirement without a scope-change row, without a decision_ref, and without the delta edges the protocol requires. The operator would be agreeing to something the option did not name. This is the same failure shape the project already records at the measurement layer (a control that cannot see its subject) arriving at the INTERVIEW layer: a question that has not been checked against the register is an instrument that cannot detect the case it most needs to catch.
category: operator-interaction; interview; homework; requirement-coverage; scope-change; silent-drift
impact_if_followed: The operator decides on options that are all actually available, and a capability that already has an approved requirement behind it is never disposed of by an allowlist comment. Demonstrated the same day: once FR-030 was quoted in full with its traces, the operator picked a fourth option — explicit deferral with an activation trigger — that the original question had not even offered.
impact_if_ignored: Approved, traced requirements get abandoned invisibly, one interview at a time. The damage is in the RECORD rather than the build, which is what makes it hard to find later: FR-030 would have stayed Approved and traced to WBS-5.7 forever, reading to every future session as planned work, while the only evidence of the decision to drop it sat in a comment inside a test file. That is precisely the drift the standing rule forbids — code and package disagree and neither is fixed nor recorded.

title: A proxy is not the artifact: a register attribute, a register row, and a filename each said BUILT about code that was not
statement: Before classifying something as built, read the thing itself. Every proxy failed in one session, each time while I was correcting the previous proxy's failure: (1) the requirement register's mvp/Phase attributes said 53 requirements were 'deliberately not built' - about 30 were built and shipped, because the attributes record the ORIGINAL scoping and the P1-P19 ladder outgrew them; (2) correcting that, I trusted a DIFFERENT register row (DW-001) and a FILENAME, and reported FR-036 as built because Timeline.tsx exists; (3) reading Timeline.tsx showed a deliberate honest SHELL whose own header says 'no bars are drawn', and the same read caught Calendar.tsx as a second shell. The shells are the sharpest form of this: present, deliberate, well-commented, routed, and empty - every proxy says built, and only the file says otherwise.
context: The DW-029 classification sweep, 2026-08-18, over the 161 requirements with no acceptance criterion. The stakes were real: SC-020 would have stamped live, shipped features 'Deferred', falsifying the register in the opposite direction from the manufactured-status failure DEF-010 records - and the operator approved the reclassification twice against my counts before the shells were found.
recommendation: Classify from source, never from an attribute, a register row, or a path. Check BOTH directions - the sweep found FR-032 unbuilt inside the 'presumed built' group as well as ~30 built inside the 'presumed unbuilt' one. When a proxy is unavoidable, prefer one that is high-precision in a stated direction and say which: requirement ids cited in source comments proved strong evidence of being BUILT, but the instrument is POSITIVE-ONLY (Kanban.tsx plainly exists and is never cited) and one citation turned out to be a DEFERRAL note (InvariantStatus.cs:7). And check that the instrument can discriminate at all: slice status could not classify the 53, because all of them have slice_id NULL and the check returns one bucket whatever the truth is.
impact_if_followed: Classification reflects what exists. The sweep, done properly, also surfaced four requirements unbuilt with NO record anywhere (FR-032, FR-134, FR-154, FR-155), a decision recorded only in a code comment (FR-108/109, now DEC-062), and a deferral whose blocker had silently cleared (FR-035, now DW-037) - none of which any gate could have found.
impact_if_ignored: The register acquires false statuses that no gate can detect, in whichever direction the proxy happens to be wrong. A Deferred label on shipped work is exactly as dishonest as an Implemented label on unbuilt work, and it is harder to notice because it looks conservative.

title: A checker that reports success may have had nothing to check: prove the instrument has a subject before believing its green
statement: Before trusting a clean scan, prove the scanner actually looked at something. Inject a deliberate fault and watch the count move. A tool that exits 0 over an empty file set is indistinguishable, at the exit code, from a tool that exits 0 over a clean one - and the empty case is silent by construction, so nothing will ever tell you.
context: SL-030, 2026-08-19. `npx tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json` in src/Acmp.Web exited 0 and I recorded the SPA as typechecking. It checks NOTHING: that file is solution-style - "files": [] plus three project references - so tsc resolves zero inputs and succeeds. The tree it blessed had THIRTEEN type errors and had been failing `npm run build` for ten commits (DEF-091). I only caught it because vitest failed seconds later on a change tsc had just approved; had the two agreed, I would have opened a PR asserting a typecheck that never ran. The same session had already been bitten by a sibling of this: `grep -c $'\r'` reported CRs on a pure-LF file, and a control file with one CR line reported two.
recommendation: For any gate you are about to cite as evidence - typecheck, lint, formatter, security scan, coverage - run it once with a deliberate fault present and confirm it FAILS, then remove the fault. Prefer the command CI runs (here `npm run build`) over a hand-rolled invocation, because CI's command is the one whose subject is known-good. Where a config file can be empty-by-design (solution-style tsconfig, an unmatched glob, a filter that selects nothing), treat a pass as unproven until the subject count is visible.
impact_if_followed: A cited gate means what it says. The deliberate-fault check cost about thirty seconds here and converted a false green into DEF-091, which turned out to be a HIGH-severity finding blocking the PR - ten commits of red that four sessions of green vitest runs had hidden.
impact_if_ignored: Evidence that is literally empty gets recorded as verification, in audit rows and PR bodies that later sessions read as settled. It is strictly worse than no check: an absent check invites suspicion, while a passing one closes the question.

title: Sweep the registers by KEYWORD as well as by identifier - an id-only sweep is a scan with no subject when the two rows never name each other
statement: LL-005 and its trap tell you to sweep the adr, decision and open-question registers before disposing of a capability or putting an option in front of the operator. Batch 14 did exactly that for seven candidate requirements, BY IDENTIFIER, and got ZERO hits for six of the seven. That result reads as 'the registers are silent about these' and it is wrong. The keyword sweep run immediately afterwards found decisive governing rows for THREE of them - and one of those, ADR-0035, is Approved and ratified and replaces the storage technology that NFR-027 still mandated by name. NFR-027 says MinIO. ADR-0035 says MinIO. NEITHER ROW CONTAINS THE OTHER'S IDENTIFIER ANYWHERE, so no identifier sweep could ever have connected them, however carefully it was run. THE GENERAL SHAPE: a requirement and the decision that superseded it are usually written years apart by different hands, and cross-references are added only when someone happens to notice the link - which is precisely the noticing this sweep exists to do. Identifiers are how the register refers to itself AFTER the connection is known; the SUBJECT MATTER is what they share BEFORE it is. So sweep on the nouns: the technology, the vendor, the mechanism, the surface. HOW TO APPLY: for each candidate, extract three to six subject keywords from its own statement and grep the adr, decision, open-question, constraint and invariant registers for those as well as for the id. Run BOTH - the id sweep still finds the deliberate cross-references, and it is cheap. And when the id sweep comes back empty for most of a batch, treat that emptiness as a signal the instrument is too narrow rather than as a finding about the registers.

This adds HOW to sweep them, which is the half that was still unstated - and batch 14 shows the how can silently defeat the which.", "cost_if_ignored": "Batch 14 would have written an acceptance criterion naming self-hosted MinIO, contradicting a ratified ADR, and recorded it as Met with real-looking evidence for the other three clauses. title: Two instruments agreeing is ONE instrument when they share a mechanism - corroboration requires independence, not repetition
statement: Verifying that no pre-signed URL can reach a notification, batch 14 wrote a line-based grep for the record's constructor and got 13 construction sites across 7 files. Suspecting the line-based approach, it then wrote a genuinely different instrument - a multi-line-aware argument parser that tracks brackets and string literals - and got THE SAME 13 SITES ACROSS THE SAME 7 FILES. Two independently written scanners, identical answer. That is what corroboration looks like, and it was false: both were blind to the same two builder files, because those use C# target-typed 'new(' where the type is inferred from the return type, so the string the pattern keys on never appears at the construction site at all. TWENTY PERCENT OF THE SURFACE WAS INVISIBLE TO BOTH, and their agreement made that invisibility feel confirmed. THE TEST THAT MATTERS is not 'did I check it twice' but 'do my two checks share a MECHANISM'. Both of these keyed on the same token in the same position; varying the parsing sophistication varied nothing that mattered. THE FIX WAS TO CHANGE THE SUBJECT, not the sophistication: scan every builder FILE for what must not be there - an absolute URL, a storage reference, a non-relative link helper - rather than scanning for a syntactic pattern and enumerating what it finds. A file set is countable and assertable; you can state that there are ten of them and fail if there are fewer. A syntactic pattern silently narrows and its denominator is whatever it happened to match. HOW TO APPLY: prefer an instrument whose subject is an enumerable population over one whose subject is a pattern; assert the population size before believing any result over it; and when a second instrument agrees with the first, ask what they have in common before counting it as evidence.

title: When a requirement says X shall be the single source for Y, check that X EXISTS before measuring anything about Y - a missing ruler makes the measurable half undecidable, not merely unverified
statement: NFR-039 has two clauses: the EN-AR terminology glossary shall be the SINGLE SOURCE of canonical bilingual terms, and no term shall have more than one AR translation in the application. Batch 15 was queued to verify it and the obvious move was to go straight at the second clause, because it is the mechanical one - pair the i18n resource files, group by English label, count distinct Arabic renderings. That measurement runs fine and produces a number. THE NUMBER MEANS NOTHING WITHOUT THE FIRST CLAUSE, and the first clause turned out to be false: README section G lists 22 English terms and says the Arabic pairing is finalized in the design handoff; the design handoff says the shared glossary is README section G; the archived governance glossary says the pairing lives in the design and i18n resources. THREE DOCUMENTS, ZERO ARABIC CHARACTERS BETWEEN THEM, each pointing at another. The glossary does not exist. THE CONSEQUENCE IS SHARPER THAN 'ONE CLAUSE FAILED'. Where two Arabic renderings of one English label genuinely differ, deciding which is canonical requires a canon - and there is none. So the second clause is not unverified, it is UNDECIDABLE, and a verdict citing the measurement would have looked thoroughly evidenced while resting on nothing. THE GENERAL FORM: a requirement of the shape 'X shall be the single source of truth for Y' has a DEPENDENCY ORDER, not two independent clauses. Y is only measurable relative to X. The same shape appears wherever a requirement names a policy, a standard, a glossary, a reference implementation or a baseline as the thing conformance is measured against. HOW TO APPLY: when a requirement names an authority, OPEN THE AUTHORITY FIRST - before writing any instrument for the conformance half. Confirm it exists, that it is not a pointer to something else, and that it actually contains the kind of content the requirement says it holds. If it does not, stop: the conformance half cannot be verified, no acceptance criterion can be written, and the honest instrument is a deferred-work row saying the ruler is missing. A missing authority is a DIFFERENT finding from a half-built feature and should not be filed as one.

This says read the AUTHORITY a requirement measures against before measuring - which is the same instinct applied one level up, to the requirement's own premise rather than to the artifact under test. The reason it may deserve its own row is the consequence: LL-006's failure mode is a wrong answer, this one's is a CONFIDENT answer to a question that has none.", "why_it_is_worth_a_row_at_all": "Because my own hand generalized it three times unprompted - twice into prm-next and once into the memory index - before any row existed. That is the revealed judgement that it is durable, and prose surfaces do not bind a future session.", "instances": ["NFR-039: the EN-AR glossary its second clause measures against is a circular pointer between two English documents (DW-069, batch 15)", "Near-miss of the same shape: NFR-054's minimal-base clause, where the four measured image sizes prove the OTHER clause and a verdict citing them would have covered half the requirement (DEF-096, batch 13)"]}

title: An identifier is a POINTER, not a reference - any artifact put in front of the operator must carry the full text of every entity it cites, at the point it cites it
statement: THE INSTANCE. Asked to disposition 53 open deferred-work rows, I built a slate that named roughly forty package entities by identifier alone - every DW row by number, plus DEC-064, SC-020, ADR-0022, DEC-020, ADR-0003, OQ-040, AC-049, AC-105, NFR-011, NFR-013, FR-035 and more - and then asked the operator to rule on them. The operator refused the interview and said so plainly: do not just mention an id and expect me to go and check it myself. THE FAILURE IS NOT COSMETIC AND IT IS NOT ABOUT FORMATTING. An identifier is an index into a store the reader may not have open. Citing one transfers the retrieval work to the person the artifact exists to serve, and it does it at the exact moment they are being asked to decide - so the practical effect is either a decision made on my summary of the row rather than the row, or no decision at all. Both are worse than a longer document. WHY IT IS EASY TO GET WRONG. Identifiers read as precision. A slate dense with DEC-064 and ADR-0022 looks rigorous and traceable, and it IS traceable - for the agent, which has the store open and can resolve every one in a tool call. The asymmetry is invisible from my side: I had already read all 53 rows, so the ids felt like references. To the reader they were homework. This is the same shape as writing a tally from memory - the information was in front of me once, and I assumed the artifact carried it. THE GENERAL FORM. An artifact intended for a human decision is self-contained or it is not a decision artifact. Traceability and legibility are different properties: the id gives traceability, the quoted text gives legibility, and a decision needs both. HOW TO APPLY. When producing anything the operator will read to decide - a slate, an interview, a disposition list, a report, a recommendation - every entity referenced carries its own text where it is referenced: title, the operative field (a deferred-work row's activation trigger, a decision's decision clause, an ADR's decision, a requirement's statement, an acceptance criterion's given/when/then), its lifecycle status, and its provenance. Quote it verbatim from the canonical JSONL, never a paraphrase and never re-typed by hand - generate it, the way any other payload is generated. Collapse it if the volume hurts scanning, but the text must be ON the page and not one lookup away. The test is mechanical: could a reader who has never opened this package adjudicate every question in the artifact using only the artifact? If not, it is not finished.

LL-001 governs how a generated payload reaches the STORE - paste it, never re-type it. This governs how store content reaches the OPERATOR - quote it, never merely cite it. Both fail when a human hand stands between a canonical text and its destination.", "relationship_to_LL-003": "LL-003 says start the operator interview immediately when something is theirs to decide. This adds the precondition: an interview whose questions cite entities the operator cannot read from the artifact is not ready to start, however promptly it is offered.", "scope_note": "Applies to operator-facing artifacts, not to agent-internal reasoning or to progress entries and verdict evidence, where an id is the correct compact reference and the reader is a session with the store open."}

title: A MUTATION CHECK HAS TWO SUBJECTS, AND 'the mutant passed' cannot tell 'no test exists' from 'the test did not fire' - the TEST COUNT is what disambiguates them
statement: SUPERSEDED BY LL-013 on the operator's instruction of 2026-08-21: merge this into LL-007 rather than carry a second row. Because the store refuses in-place edits of an approved lesson, the merge is expressed as LL-013 superseding BOTH this row and LL-007. The content is preserved there in full. It was never approved and therefore never bound a session; LL-013 is the row that binds.

The operator asked whether the pattern was a lesson, which is what prompted checking the existing register rather than assuming.", "relationship_to_LL-007": "REFINEMENT, not a duplicate - and specifically it closes LL-007's own blind spot. LL-007 prescribes injecting a deliberate fault to prove a scanner had a subject. That is exactly what was done here, and it still produced a false green, because LL-007 inspects the FAULT and not the DETECTOR. Anyone reading LL-007 alone would believe they had discharged the risk.", "relationship_to_LL-009": "Adjacent but different. LL-009 is about two instruments AGREEING while sharing a mechanism - a corroboration failure with two detectors present. This is a case with ONE detector that was ABSENT, where its absence and its silence look identical.", "the_disambiguator": "The test count. It moved from 10 to 13 only after the file was actually written, and that number - not the mutant's verdict - is what proved the instrument existed.", "honest_note": "The check did work: the passing mutant was flagged as suspicious rather than accepted, and investigating it found the cause. The lesson is not that the instinct failed, it is that the instinct should not have to carry it - the count check is cheap and mechanical and should be routine."}

title: A checker that reports success may have had nothing to check: prove the instrument has a subject - and when the instrument IS an injected fault, prove the detector exists too
statement:
Before trusting a clean scan, prove the scanner actually looked at something. Inject a deliberate fault and watch the count move. A tool that exits 0 over an empty file set is indistinguishable, at the exit code, from a tool that exits 0 over a clean one - and the empty case is silent by construction, so nothing will ever tell you.

THE REMEDY ABOVE HAS THE BLIND SPOT IT WAS WRITTEN TO CLOSE, ONE LEVEL UP. 'Inject a deliberate fault and watch the count move' treats the SCANNER as the thing that might lack a subject. It proves the FAULT was injected. It says nothing about whether the DETECTOR exists.

A MUTATION CHECK STACKS TWO INSTRUMENTS - the mutant, and the test meant to catch it - and the sentence above inspects only one. Fixing DEF-103 I wrote three tests for a truncation notice, mutated its condition to always-true to prove they were load-bearing, and the suite PASSED. A passing mutant reads as 'my tests do not cover this': a normal, unalarming result whose natural next move is to write more tests or shrug. Neither would have found the truth - the test file had never been written at all. A `cd` earlier in the same chained shell command failed, so the heredoc that wrote the tests never ran, while the vitest invocation on the NEXT line ran anyway and printed a healthy count. I was reading ten PRE-EXISTING tests and calling it a mutation result.

THE ASYMMETRY IS THE WHOLE THING. A mutant that FAILS is self-proving: something ran, saw the fault, objected. A mutant that PASSES proves nothing whatsoever, because a missing test, a mis-targeted file, a filtered-out test, a stale build and a genuinely uncovered branch all produce the IDENTICAL observation. And it is the direction that FEELS like a completed check, because you did the work of writing the mutant.

HOW TO APPLY, and it costs one command. For any gate you are about to cite as evidence - typecheck, lint, formatter, security scan, coverage - run it once with a deliberate fault present and confirm it FAILS, then remove the fault. Prefer the command CI runs over a hand-rolled invocation, because CI's command is the one whose subject is known-good. Where a config can be empty-by-design (a solution-style tsconfig, an unmatched glob, a filter that selects nothing), treat a pass as unproven until the subject count is visible. AND WHEN THE GATE IS A MUTATION CHECK, count twice: prove the detector exists before mutating - the test count moved from ten to thirteen - then require the count of FAILURES to move under the mutant. Two counts, both moving, in both directions. 'Thirteen tests where there were ten, of which two fail under the mutant' is a verified check; 'the mutant passed' is not a result at all. The same applies to any layered instrument where one layer detects a fault in another: a linter rule and the file that should trip it, a schema and the payload that should violate it, a guard and the call that should be refused.

A MECHANISM WORTH KEEPING SEPARATELY, because it is not specific to tests: in a multi-command invocation an early step can fail while a later step still runs and prints a healthy-looking number. The output you read may come from a step that ran while the step that mattered did not - the same family as reading an exit status after a pipe and getting the pipe's last command instead of your gate's. WHEN A COMMAND CHAIN WRITES SOMETHING AND THEN MEASURES IT, THE MEASUREMENT IS NOT EVIDENCE THAT THE WRITE HAPPENED.
context: Merged row. The first half is LL-007 (SL-030, 2026-08-19): `npx tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json` in src/Acmp.Web exited 0 and I recorded the SPA as typechecking. It checks NOTHING - that file is solution-style, "files": [] plus three project references, so tsc resolves zero inputs and succeeds. The tree it blessed had THIRTEEN type errors and had been failing `npm run build` for ten commits (DEF-091). I only caught it because vitest failed seconds later on a change tsc had just approved; had the two agreed, I would have opened a PR asserting a typecheck that never ran. The second half is LL-012 (SL-032 / DEF-103, 2026-08-21), where the FIRST half's own remedy produced a false green.
recommendation: Run every cited gate once with a deliberate fault present and confirm it FAILS, then remove the fault. Prefer CI's command over a hand-rolled one. Where a config can select nothing by design, treat a pass as unproven until the subject count is visible. For a mutation check specifically, prove the DETECTOR exists first by watching the test count move, then watch the failure count move under the mutant - a passing mutant is not a result.
impact_if_followed: A cited gate means what it says. The deliberate-fault check cost about thirty seconds and converted a false green into DEF-091, a HIGH-severity finding blocking a PR - ten commits of red that four sessions of green vitest runs had hidden. The added count check cost one command and caught a mutation result that was measuring a test file which did not exist.
impact_if_ignored: Evidence that is literally empty gets recorded as verification, in audit rows and PR bodies that later sessions read as settled. It is strictly worse than no check: an absent check invites suspicion, while a passing one closes the question. And with a stacked instrument the failure is quieter still, because the outer check LOOKS like the diligence that would have caught it.

title: Two libraries implementing the SAME technique are not interchangeable evidence - 'the technique works here' and 'this package works here' are different claims, and registry metadata cannot tell them apart
statement:
THE INSTANCE. WBS-23.3's spike had a dependency evaluation already done and carried into the session as settled: four DOM-to-image packages ranked on registry metadata - unpacked size, runtime dependency count, weekly downloads, last-published date - with the instruction 'THE DEPENDENCY EVALUATION IS DONE - do not redo it' and the pick marked. All four implement the identical technique: clone the node, serialise it into an SVG foreignObject, load that as a data-URL image, draw it to a canvas. Under this app's shipped CSP the technique runs clean. The PICKED package does not. `modern-screenshot` 4.7.0 throws on every capture because `embedWebFont` creates a scratch document via `implementation.createHTMLDocument()`, appends a `<style>` to it, and dereferences `.sheet` unguarded - and that scratch document inherits the page's CSP, so the sheet is null. `html-to-image`, rejected on the metadata as the largest and stalest candidate, appends its font `<style>` to the DETACHED clone instead and works with zero violations. The ranking inverted completely against the only axis that decides anything.

THE RULE. When a dependency has to satisfy a hard environmental constraint - a CSP, a sandbox, an offline install, a target runtime, a licence bar - the shortlist is ordered by that constraint FIRST and by registry metadata only among the survivors. Size, dependency count and freshness rank packages that all work; they say nothing about which ones work. And a claim about a TECHNIQUE never transfers to a PACKAGE: the failure was not in the foreignObject approach at all, it was in one unguarded property read on a code path that had nothing to do for this app. That is invisible from any description of what the library does, and visible in about two minutes from running it against the real constraint.

WHY THIS IS NOT ALREADY COVERED. LL-006 says a proxy is not the artifact, about classifying something as BUILT. This is the selection case: a proxy is not the artifact when you are CHOOSING, and the specific proxy - a package registry's own summary of itself - is one that reads as hard data because every field in it is a real measured number. Every number in that table was correct. The table was still useless for the decision it was being used to make.

HOW TO APPLY. Before accepting any carried-over dependency pick, ask what the binding constraint is and whether the pick was ever run against it. If not, run the smallest thing that exercises the constraint before the package reaches package.json - here that was one built page, one real header, one card. Keep the losing candidates in the harness rather than the notes: the answer came from testing all of them in one run, and testing only the pick would have produced 'the technique is impossible here' - a conclusion that is false and that would have gone to the operator as a request to widen a security header.
impact_if_followed: A dependency that cannot satisfy the environment is found before it is installed, in one run, against the real constraint - and the alternatives are already measured, so the operator gets a decision rather than a blocker.
impact_if_ignored: The pick fails after it is installed, and because the technique looks identical across the family, the failure reads as 'the approach is impossible in this environment'. Here that would have arrived at the operator as a request to add style-src 'unsafe-inline' - reversing DW-022's recorded finding and weakening a shipped security header to work around one unguarded property read in one package.

PE-578 carries the full run.", "evidence": "modern-screenshot 4.7.0 dist/index.mjs:1347-1350 creates the scratch document, :1381 dereferences the null sheet; html-to-image 1.11.13 inserts into the real sheet and appends the font style element to the detached clone. Chromium 149.0.7827.55, both locales, three negative CSP controls fired first."}

title: A scan's SCOPE is part of its answer - a scanner that runs, has a subject, and returns a true number about the wrong SET reads exactly like a finding, and LL-013's fault-injection cannot catch it
statement:
THREE INSTANCES IN ONE DAY, each of which looked like a real result. (a) Sweeping for uncapped paged reads, I keyed on the identifier `PageSize` and got TEN; sweeping every `.Take(...)` found TWELVE - the audit endpoint and `GetDecisions` page with locals named `size` and `n`. (b) Probing whether a library really embeds fonts, my regex counted `url(data:` and reported `dataUrlCount: 0` beside an 874,619-character string; the URLs are quoted, so the true count was 48. (c) Reviewing a claim that a test exists to stop drag-reorder regressing to a swap, I grepped `tests/ --include=*.cs` and got ZERO - which reads as the claim being false. The tests are real; they live in the SPA under `src/` and in a C# file under different naming.

WHY LL-013 DOES NOT COVER IT, and this is the whole point of a separate row. LL-013 says prove the scanner looked at something: inject a deliberate fault and watch the count move. In all three cases here the scanner DID look at something, the count DID move, and the number returned was TRUE - of a set that excluded the answer. Injecting a fault into `tests/*.cs` would have been found and would have confirmed a scanner that was already structurally blind. LL-013 guards against an instrument with no subject; this guards against an instrument with the WRONG subject.

THE RULE. Before believing a scan, state its DENOMINATOR out loud and ask what it excludes: which file types, which directories, which spellings, which quoting. A zero is the most dangerous result, because absence is what people act on - and the three cheap discriminators are (1) widen the pattern to the CONCEPT rather than one identifier and see whether the count moves, (2) run the same question a second way that shares no mechanism with the first, and (3) sanity-check the result against something you already know: an `874,619-character string containing zero data URLs` is incoherent on its face, and noticing that is what caught (b).

HOW TO APPLY. Report the denominator with the finding - 'twelve of fourteen paged reads' not 'twelve uncapped reads' - so a reader can see what was searched. When a scan returns ZERO for something a record claims exists, treat the SCAN as the prime suspect before the record: two of the three instances here were me nearly contradicting a true statement in the register.
impact_if_followed: A narrow sweep is caught while it is still a sweep, before its number reaches a defect row, a verdict or an artifact the operator reads. Findings carry their denominator, so a reader can judge coverage instead of trusting it.
impact_if_ignored: A true number about the wrong set is indistinguishable from a finding, and it points the wrong way in both directions: it under-reports real work (ten uncapped reads instead of twelve) and it manufactures false findings against correct records (a guard test reported as missing when it exists). The second is worse - it invites 'fixing' something that was never broken, or filing a defect against a record that was right.

The three instances are PE-579/DEF-104's first sweep, the getFontEmbedCSS probe in PE-578, and the AC-141 guard check during the review itself.", "relationship_to_LL-013": "Complementary, not overlapping. LL-013 = the scanner had NO subject. This = the scanner had the WRONG subject. Fault injection detects the first and confirms the second."}

title: A sequence in prose is invisible to every mechanical check, and a phrase can go stale without its number changing - the wrong half travels attached to a figure you did just measure, which is what makes it invisible
statement: A sequence in prose is invisible to every mechanical check - an id-and-status pass sees ids and statuses, never an ordinal. And a phrase can go stale without its number changing: "nine families" was carried whole out of an older sentence with only the figure in front of it refreshed, so the false half travelled attached to a number I had genuinely just measured - which is exactly what made it invisible.
context: 2026-08-23, preparing the durable kickoff prompt for a fresh session. THE FIRST HALF: the file's own section counting the times it has carried a stale statement had TWO different findings, added by two different commits, both labelled THE THIRTEENTH - so its counter was a whole occasion short and there was no fourteenth at all. A mechanical pass over 190 identifiers ran clean straight past it, because an ordinal is not an identifier and no gate has an opinion about a numbering. THE SECOND HALF happened inside the repair. Writing up that finding, I asserted the 190 identifiers spanned 'nine families'. Nothing had measured that; the phrase came whole out of the same file's TENTH entry - '68 across nine families' - with only the figure in front of it refreshed. Measured, it is fifteen. It reached three durable places including a pushed commit message that cannot be amended, and it sat INSIDE the sentence asserting the mechanical pass had run clean. An independent review pass caught it, not me and not any gate. PE-593 carried it; PE-595 corrects it.
recommendation: Treat the WORDS around a number as unverified until you have measured them too, especially when you have just measured the number - that freshness is what launders the rest of the sentence. When reusing a sentence's shape from anywhere, re-derive every claim in it rather than refreshing the figures, because the shape is where the stale part hides. And when a durable artifact carries an ordered sequence - numbered findings, versioned entries, a lettered ladder - check the sequence itself for gaps and collisions, since no foreign-key check, id sweep or status pass will ever look at it.
rationale: This project's controls are strong at exactly one thing: identifiers and their statuses. Every instrument it has built - G-IDS, the entity index, the id-and-status sweep - answers 'does this id exist and is its status what you said'. Prose sits outside all of them, and the parts of prose that look most like data are the parts that get least scrutiny, because a number reads as though something produced it. An ordinal and a carried phrase are both prose wearing the costume of a measured fact.
impact_if_followed: The half of a durable artifact that no gate can see gets read as deliberately as the half that gates check, and sequences stay countable. The cheap tell is available every time: if a clause would survive being deleted without changing the claim, it was never load-bearing and should not be there; if it would not, it needs measuring in the same breath as the number beside it.
impact_if_ignored: A false clause rides into a commit message on the back of a true number and cannot be amended afterwards, which is how this one escaped. Worse, it lands preferentially in the sentences that assert a check ran clean - so the artifact's own claim to have been verified is the place least likely to have been.

title: When an instrument changes and the numbers get worse, 'the new instrument is broken' and 'the old instrument was lying' produce identical evidence - only reading the disputed measurement by hand separates them
statement: A tool upgrade that makes measurements worse is ambiguous in a way that feels resolved but is not. The new instrument may be miscounting, or the old one may have been crediting things it should not have - and BOTH hypotheses predict exactly the same observation: numbers dropped, code unchanged. Trap 2 says a measurement that indicts known-good code is measuring itself, and that heuristic is correct and useful; but it has a converse that must be checked before it is applied, because sometimes the code was not as good as the old measurement said. The discriminator is always the same and it is cheap: shrink the disagreement down to ONE artefact small enough to adjudicate by hand, get both instruments' detailed output for it, and read the disputed item yourself.
context: 2026-08-23. Upgrading @vitest/coverage-v8 from 3.2.6 to 4.1.11 dropped about twenty files below ADR-0016's 95% line threshold while every test still passed and no source file changed. It read exactly like a broken instrument, and the deferred-work row filed for it said so. The experiment: same source, same test file, same three passing tests, coverage under v3 then v4, over a 55-line component chosen because it could be counted by hand. v3 reported 100% lines and nothing uncovered; v4 reported 90% and named exactly one line. That line held a Button whose onClick was an inline arrow; the tests rendered it but never clicked it. BOTH providers' function maps recorded the same uncalled function - they differed only in whether an uninvoked callback makes its LINE uncovered. Since the gate is lines-only by explicit design, v3 had been rendering every untested inline handler invisible to it. The twenty files were never properly covered.
recommendation: Before concluding that a new instrument is wrong, find the smallest artefact on which the two instruments disagree, obtain each one's detailed per-item output rather than its summary percentage, and adjudicate the disputed item by reading the code. Prefer an artefact you can count by hand over a representative one. If both instruments turn out to AGREE on the underlying facts and differ only in how they aggregate them, the question is not which is correct in general but which aggregation matches what the gate claims to measure - and that is answerable from the gate's own definition.
rationale: The two hypotheses are observationally identical at the summary level, which is the only level anyone normally looks at. A percentage cannot distinguish 'wrongly counted' from 'previously miscredited'. Detailed output can, because instruments usually agree about raw execution and disagree about attribution - and attribution is checkable against the code.
impact_if_followed: A tool upgrade that exposes a real gap gets treated as the discovery it is, and the gap gets closed. Governance thresholds keep meaning what they say, because the question 'which aggregation matches the gate's own definition' gets asked out loud instead of settled by whichever number is more convenient.
impact_if_ignored: The comfortable reading wins, because it is also the cheaper one: the new tool is blamed, the upgrade is refused or the threshold is quietly lowered, and code that has never been executed by any test keeps counting as covered. The register then records a number that is true about the measurement and false about the software.

title: Two runners exercising one shared artefact are ONE instrument for locating a fault and TWO for verifying its repair - LL-009 applies to the shared component, not to the harnesses around it
statement: LL-009 says two instruments agreeing is one instrument when they share a mechanism. The trap in applying it is that superficial difference feels like independence: a different test runner, a different orchestrator, a different machine. None of that is independence if both paths build or load the SAME artefact - the thing under test is identical and only the scaffolding differs. But the relationship is asymmetric, and the second half is worth as much as the first: the very same pair of observations that is WEAK evidence about WHERE a fault lives is STRONG evidence that a change to their shared component WORKED. Independence matters for localising a cause. It matters much less for verifying a repair to the thing they share.
context: 2026-08-23. A dependency bump of the SQL Server base image failed under Testcontainers and, identically, under docker-compose. I read two execution paths agreeing as independent corroboration and concluded the fault was in the vendor's image, recording that production must not move to that version. Both paths build the project's own Dockerfile. The vendor images were fine - ldd reported nothing missing in either - and the real cause was a hardcoded package-repo URL in that shared Dockerfile, which installed a package built for the old base onto the new one. I had quoted LL-009 earlier in the same session before walking into it. When the coupled fix landed, those same two paths both went green, and that confirmation was worth MORE than the failure had been, because the change was made in the component they both exercise.
recommendation: Before calling two failing observations independent corroboration, ask what artefact each one actually loads, not what tooling drives it. If the answer is the same file, the same image or the same build, you have one observation twice and you have learned nothing about where the fault is. Conversely, once you have changed that shared artefact, those same two paths are a good verification precisely because they both depend on it - so do not discount a repair's confirmation on the grounds that the observers were not independent.
rationale: Independence is a property of what is being measured, not of who is measuring. Two harnesses over one artefact vary everything except the variable that matters. The asymmetry follows: for localisation you need observations that could have differed, and these could not; for verification you need observations that would have failed if the change did not work, and these would.
impact_if_followed: Fault localisation stops being decided by a coincidence of tooling, and repairs to shared components get the credit their confirmation deserves. A wrong conclusion about where a fault lives - the kind that reaches a production recommendation - gets caught before it is recorded.
impact_if_ignored: A shared artefact's defect gets attributed to whatever lies beyond it, most often a vendor, and the resulting statement is both wrong and expensive: it forecloses an upgrade that was never the problem, and it leaves the real coupling in place to fire again on the next bump.

title: A pinned base image and a pinned package repository are ONE decision expressed in two places, and only one of them is automated - so an automated bump can never go green alone
statement: Where a Dockerfile pins a base image AND separately configures a package repository whose URL encodes the same platform - a distribution release, a product major, an architecture - those two lines are a single decision written twice. Dependency bots update the one they understand and cannot see the other, so their pull request installs packages built for the old platform onto the new one and fails in ways that look like the vendor's fault. The general form is broader than containers: any pair of version-bearing values that must agree, where only one has an automated updater, will drift the first time the updater runs. The fix is not to distrust the bot; it is to put the coupling where the next person editing either line will read it, because a register entry is a record and a comment beside the line is a control.
context: 2026-08-23. A Dependabot pull request bumped a SQL Server base image from one major to the next, changing only the FROM line. The Dockerfile installs full-text search - required by the product's search requirements and carrying a language-specific word-breaker - from a hardcoded repository URL naming the OLD distribution release and the OLD product major. That package pulls in the database server itself, so the bump installed the old platform's server binary over the new image's own, leaving a binary linked against a library the new base does not ship. The pull request had been open five weeks and could never have gone green. The fix moved both lines together and added a comment above them saying they are one decision.
recommendation: When a build file pins a base image, grep the same file for any other line carrying a distribution release, a product major or an architecture, and treat every such pair as one decision. Write the coupling as a comment immediately above the lines rather than only into a tracking row. When a bot's bump of one of them fails, check the pair before concluding anything about the upstream artefact.
rationale: Automated updaters operate on the syntax they were built to recognise, not on the semantics of the file. A FROM line is recognisable; a version embedded in a URL is not. The asymmetry is structural and will not be fixed by the bot, so it has to be absorbed by whoever reads the file - which means the warning has to live where they are already looking.
impact_if_followed: A base-image bump either lands complete or fails for a reason that is immediately legible, and the next person to edit either line is told about the other by the file itself rather than by a register they may never open.
impact_if_ignored: The bot's pull request sits red indefinitely and is eventually dismissed as an upstream problem, which is both wrong and costly: it blocks a platform upgrade that was always available, and the diagnosis lands on a vendor who did nothing wrong.

title: A CORRECTED MEASUREMENT DOES NOT CORRECT THE INFERENCE SOMEBODY BUILT ON IT
statement: When a wrong number is fixed, the CONCLUSIONS drawn from it while it was wrong do not travel with the fix. They stay where they were written, now detached from the evidence that produced them, and they read exactly like conclusions drawn from the corrected number. Fixing a measurement is therefore only half the repair: the other half is finding what was inferred from the old value and re-deriving it.
context: DW-082. Version one of the coverage triage script scraped vitest's ASCII table and misread TopBar's compressed 'Uncovered Line #s' cell of '92-138' as a 47-line range; the structured data says seven lines. From that wrong size an explanation was reasoned out - that TopBar's cause could not be untested handlers, and must instead be the DevRoleSwitcher coverage-exclusion asymmetry charging TopBar for a branch the exclusion hides. Version two of the script corrected the NUMBER to seven. Nobody re-derived the CAUSE. The wrong explanation then travelled into PE-610, into PE-611, into prm-next.md's next-action block, and into the memory index as a standing warning that this file 'is NOT a handler fix; it needs its own decision'. Measured on 2026-08-25: all seven of TopBar's uncovered lines are ordinary inline handlers, the lazy() declaration records three hits, and the call site has no statement starting on it, so it never enters the line metric at all. The exclusion charges TopBar nothing.
recommendation: When you correct a measurement, immediately search for what was CONCLUDED from the old one - in your own notes, in the register, in any prompt or handoff - and re-derive each conclusion from the new value rather than assuming the fix propagated. Treat the correction as incomplete until that sweep is done. Where a conclusion cannot be cheaply re-derived, mark it as resting on a superseded measurement rather than leaving it standing.
rationale: A stale NUMBER is at least in tension with the world and can be caught by re-measuring. A stale INFERENCE is well-formed prose that no gate, no id-and-status pass and no re-measurement can see, because the number it depended on is no longer present in it. It has also, by then, usually been summarised once or twice - and each summary strips the provenance that would let a reader notice it was built on something withdrawn. In this instance the wrong inference was on its way to costing an operator interview for a decision that did not exist.
impact_if_followed: A corrected measurement closes out completely, and downstream artifacts stop carrying explanations whose evidence has been withdrawn.
impact_if_ignored: Withdrawn evidence keeps producing live instructions. Sessions act on a cause that was never real - scheduling ceremonies, asking for decisions, or avoiding work - and the mechanical checks all pass, because an ordinal, an instruction and a causal claim are invisible to every one of them.

title: A COMMAND CHAIN FAILS CLOSED FOR THE COMMAND THAT BREAKS AND OPEN FOR EVERY COMMAND THAT READS A FILE THE CHAIN WAS SUPPOSED TO WRITE
statement: In `A && B && C`, a failure in A stops the chain - but only for the commands that RUN. Any later command that would have consumed A's output can still succeed on a stale copy of that output left behind by an earlier, unrelated run. The guard protects sequencing, not freshness, and a shared scratch directory silently supplies the missing input.
context: DW-082, 2026-08-25. The chain was `git add src/Acmp.Web && cat > /tmp/c4.txt <<EOF ... EOF && git commit -F /tmp/c4.txt`. The `git add` failed because the shell's working directory was already inside src/Acmp.Web, so the heredoc that writes the commit message NEVER RAN. A later invocation from the repo root then re-ran the commit step against /tmp/c4.txt - which existed, left over from an unrelated session on 2026-08-19 - and git committed the correct FILES under a commit message describing a different feature on a different branch. Nothing errored. The commit was found only by reading `git log` afterwards and noticing the subject was somebody else's commit summary.
recommendation: Write generated inputs to a path unique to the run - `/tmp/name-$$.txt` or a session directory - and delete it after use, so a stale copy cannot be adopted. Where a command consumes a file another step was supposed to produce, either generate and consume it in ONE command, or assert the file's freshness before reading it. And read back what a write-then-consume chain actually produced: `git log -1 --format=%s` costs nothing.
rationale: The failure mode is invisible precisely because every individual command behaved correctly. `git commit -F` cannot know the file it was handed is not the file the author meant; it has no way to distinguish a stale artifact from a fresh one. Commit messages are also unamendable once pushed, which is why this project already counts assertions that escaped into them - and a message describing unrelated work is worse than a vague one, because it will be believed.
impact_if_followed: A broken chain produces no commit rather than a confidently mislabelled one, and the durable record says what actually happened.
impact_if_ignored: Shared scratch paths turn a broken pipeline into a plausible-looking result. In git specifically, the wrong text becomes permanent the moment it is pushed.

title: WHEN YOU WRAP AN EXISTING FAILURE TO MAKE IT LEGIBLE, THE FAILURE IS NOT YOURS - ONLY THE MESSAGE IS. ANY ASSERTION THAT WOULD STILL HOLD AGAINST THE UNWRAPPED ORIGINAL IS TESTING THE FRAMEWORK, NOT YOUR CHANGE
statement:
A whole class of work here does not CREATE a failure, it IMPROVES one that already happens: a timeout that already fires but says nothing useful, an exception that already throws but names no context, an error already logged without the identifier that would let anyone act on it. For that class, the failing behaviour is inherited and the DIFFERENCE is the entire deliverable - so the test must assert the difference. An assertion that would pass identically against the un-improved original is asserting the framework's behaviour and reporting it as proof of yours.

THE INSTANCE (`DW-084`, PR `#309`, 2026-08-25). The change wraps a Testcontainers container start in a `CancellationTokenSource` so a hung container fails fast with the container's own log attached, instead of being retried until the CI job hits its 25-minute ceiling and reports `cancelled` - a verdict that is neither pass nor fail. The forcing test asserted three things: that a `TimeoutException` is thrown, that its message names the bound, and that it carries a marker the container printed. Mutating the wrapper away - rethrowing the raw exception - showed that Testcontainers ALREADY throws `TimeoutException`, carrying the message 'The operation has timed out.'. The type assertion had been inherited from the framework all along and would have gone green with the entire guard deleted.

WHY IT IS NOT COVERED BY `LL-013`, and the distinction is exact rather than pedantic. `LL-013` is about a mutant that PASSES: proof of nothing, because a missing test, a stale build and an uncovered branch all look identical. Here the mutant FAILED - the self-proving direction - and the check worked. What the failure revealed was not a missing detector but a MIS-ATTRIBUTED one: an assertion that was live, load-bearing in appearance, and satisfied by code nobody in this repository wrote. `LL-013` asks whether the detector exists. This asks whose behaviour the detector is detecting.

WHY IT IS EASY TO MISS. Asserting on an exception TYPE reads as more rigorous than asserting on a message - types are structural, messages are brittle prose - so the instinct that produces the vacuous assertion is the same instinct that usually produces a good one. And the type assertion is not wrong, merely inherited: it will never fail spuriously, which is exactly why it will never fail usefully either.
context: DW-084 / DEC-077 d4/d5, 2026-08-25. The row required proof by FORCING the failure rather than by a green run, because the hang it guards against is intermittent. Forcing it produced a passing test; mutating the guard away is what showed one of that test's three assertions was inherited from Testcontainers rather than earned by the change.
recommendation: Before believing a test over a make-it-better change, ask what the code did BEFORE and delete the improvement in a scratch mutation. Every assertion that still passes is measuring the pre-existing behaviour and must be treated as scaffolding, not evidence. Keep those assertions if they document intent, but never cite them as the proof. Then name the delta in words - 'the message now carries the container name, the bound, and the log' - and write one assertion per clause of that sentence. In practice this means preferring an assertion on the ADDED CONTENT (a marker, an identifier, a bound) over an assertion on the failure's shape, precisely when the failure's shape was not yours to begin with.
rationale: Improving a diagnostic is one of the few changes where the observable being asserted on existed before the change did. Everywhere else, the thing under test would not happen at all without the code being tested, so a type-or-shape assertion is automatically discriminating. That structural difference is invisible at the point of writing the test - the test looks like every other test - and the mutation is the only cheap thing that exposes it.
impact_if_followed: A guard added to make a failure legible is proven by the legibility it added, so deleting the guard reddens the suite. The test keeps its value when the framework's own behaviour changes underneath it.
impact_if_ignored: A test that would pass with the entire change reverted is filed as evidence that the change works. The guard can then be lost in a refactor or a dependency upgrade with the suite staying green - the silent-loss shape this project already treats as the most expensive kind.
